segments.title: Containerized missiles meet merchant-ship reality
segments.summary: The opening tests a missile-armed container ship against visibility, better major-power strike options, and the difficulty of controlling a civilian crew.
segments.body: Much-shared imagery of a missile-armed container ship offers a poor covert-strike option for a major power that already has submarines and regular warships. Visible launchers and radars, unusually new containers, and an implausibly light cargo would make the ship conspicuous. A smaller hidden launcher could have niche value on one controlled voyage, provided the operator also controls the crew and power supply. Engineers, bridge staff, deck hands, and stewards could all disclose the mission or disrupt it. Replacing the commercial crew with sailors introduces a different risk because naval personnel may lack experience with the ship's machinery and operating practices.

evidence.note: The opening argues that a lightly loaded container ship with visible weapons is neither an efficient nor a covert major-power strike option.
The niche single-launcher case leads into crew loyalty, merchant-engine expertise, communications, and willingness to enter danger.

segments.title: Why a wheeled modular EMALS is aspirational
segments.summary: The advertised flight-deck concept runs into alignment, maintenance, deck-clearance, and aircraft-handling problems before it becomes a practical merchant conversion.
segments.body: The proposed electromagnetic catapult is assembled from several wheeled modules, which would have to maintain the exact alignment required by EMALS. Fixed installations already demand precise construction and maintenance on purpose-built carriers. A rocket-powered launcher or a catapult contained on one vehicle would be more credible. The illustrated UAVs also need a crane or other handling arrangement that the promotional image omits. Lateral movement during launch, or a brief dip after leaving the rail, could send an aircraft into the ship's structure.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts a multi-vehicle electromagnetic catapult with the precision and maintenance needs of fixed EMALS installations.
The UAV discussion identifies missing handling gear, unsafe launch geometry, and the gap between an advertisement and a practical system.

segments.title: A missile container must survive the loading system
segments.summary: A concealed launcher depends on manifest control, one-voyage planning, port handling, and disposal as much as it depends on the missile itself.
segments.body: A single missile container could give a smaller power an unusual strike option, although it could not simply enter ordinary liner service. The operator would need close control of the crew, manifest, power connection, stack position, and route so that another container does not block or damage the launcher. Even computerized ports sometimes move or stack the wrong box because loading orders, trains, weather, and simultaneous cargo operations introduce errors. A plausible mission would use one controlled voyage, launch once, and perhaps discard the container overboard. Routine port logistics become part of weapon reliability and operational security.

evidence.note: The transcript links launcher viability to crew control, manifest influence, stack position, and the reality of container-handling mistakes.
A single-trip launch and disposal scenario is contrasted with the visually striking but impractical advertised ship.

segments.title: Merchant auxiliaries become part of the kill chain
segments.summary: Strategic lift, survey, intelligence, depot, patrol, mining, and drone-support ships all need protection because sensors and commanders are targets too.
segments.body: Merchant hulls could provide strategic lift, helicopter and depot support, patrol, survey, intelligence, covert work, minelaying, or drone support. Long-range warfare puts their information-gathering roles inside the combat zone, where distance alone no longer protects them. An enemy can disrupt a force by attacking its observers and commanders instead of concentrating on its shooters. British carrier operations and F-35B range debates illustrate why submarines, aircraft, and other assets may have to suppress hostile reconnaissance. Ships devoted to sensing or support still need escorts or credible self-defence.

evidence.note: The transcript lists plausible merchant-ship roles and explains why distant information assets now operate inside the combat zone.
The looker-shooter discussion connects reconnaissance suppression with the survivability of carrier and auxiliary forces.

segments.title: Specialization shrinks the pool of wartime auxiliaries
segments.summary: Modern warships and merchant ships are both highly specialized, making the general-purpose auxiliary conversions of earlier wars harder to reproduce.
segments.body: Earlier fleets could draw on packet ships and other general-purpose merchant vessels that combined passengers and freight. Modern warships have specialized around sensors, computers, power, personnel, and support needs. Commercial operators have likewise specialized their hulls for economic efficiency, leaving fewer ships that can become general auxiliaries without extensive modification. Just-in-time purchasing works for businesses that can buy replacements on an open market, while warships, aircraft, and their spares have lead times measured in years. Government reserves and mobilization plans must account for those delays.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts historic general-purpose merchant ships with increasingly specialized warships.
Commercial specialization and just-in-time purchasing are compared with the long lead times of defence equipment and spares.

segments.title: A brigade needs both troops and vehicles
segments.summary: Large cruise ships and vehicle carriers could move a brigade-scale force together while preserving scarce military airlift for other missions.
segments.body: Passenger aircraft can move troops quickly, but vehicles and heavy equipment still require sealift unless they were pre-positioned. A large roll-on/roll-off vehicle carrier such as Tønsberg can carry thousands of metres of vehicle lanes, while Icon of the Seas can accommodate 7,600 passengers and make 22 knots. Together, ships of those types could move a NATO brigade's personnel and vehicles. Moving the main body by sea also preserves transport aircraft for medical evacuation, replacements, spares, and other urgent tasks. Strategic lift therefore depends on combined air and sea capacity.

evidence.note: The transcript explains why troops flown without heavy equipment still depend on large vehicle carriers.
Icon of the Seas passenger capacity and speed are combined with roll-on/roll-off lift to outline a brigade-scale movement.

segments.title: From armed merchant cruiser to defensible merchant vessel
segments.summary: Large, scarce transports need enough last-mile defence to let a limited escort force protect the convoy as a whole.
segments.body: Concentrating a brigade in a few large merchant hulls creates lucrative targets and exposes the limits of a small escort fleet. Close-in weapon systems, short-range missiles such as CAMM or ESSM, useful sensors, torpedo decoys, and perhaps anti-torpedo torpedoes could give each transport some protection. Modern shipping has fewer and much larger ships than the individually armed merchantmen of the world wars, so losing one hull carries greater consequences. Each merchant vessel would defend the final mile around itself. Escorts could then concentrate on protecting the convoy or task group.

evidence.note: The transcript proposes close-in weapons, short-range air defence, sensors, torpedo decoys, and anti-torpedo systems for large transports.
Fewer, larger merchant ships lead to the concept of a defensible merchant vessel that supports rather than replaces its escorts.

segments.title: Strategic tankers keep bases supplied
segments.summary: Slow tankers moving fuel between bases can be as important as fast fleet replenishment ships, but suitable commercial hulls are increasingly specialized.
segments.body: At the start of the Second World War, many Royal Navy tankers were slow because their job was to move fuel between bases rather than accompany the fleet. Those economical voyages kept regional fleets supplied and made the bases usable. Modern commercial economics favors ever-larger or more specialized tankers, and only some can carry the fuel products that ships or land forces need. Hulls with suitable tanks, cargo compatibility, and size would become critical during a prolonged war. Strategic fuel distribution between bases is a different task from high-speed underway replenishment.

evidence.note: The transcript explains the use of slower Royal Navy tankers to move fuel between bases during the Second World War.
Commercial tanker size and specialization limit the pool able to carry the fuel products a wartime force needs.

segments.title: Old stern-to-bow refuelling still works
segments.summary: A civilian tanker can refuel warships with a slow stern-to-bow rig whose simplicity is easy to overlook beside modern alongside replenishment gear.
segments.body: Some commercial tankers can be adapted to refuel warships without the elaborate rigs fitted to purpose-built replenishment ships. In the older stern-to-bow method, the receiving ship follows in line while a hose hangs from a cable between the vessels. The transfer is slow, awkward, and lower capacity than modern alongside replenishment, but it demands much less structural modification. Engineers would still have to identify strong attachment points and fit the necessary rings or hard points. This simple system remains available in an emergency even though peacetime fleets rarely practice it.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts minimal stern-to-bow hose transfer with complex modern alongside replenishment rigs.
The discussion covers improvised strong points, engineering judgment, surviving design standards, and the persistence of old fittings.

segments.title: Tankers carry environmental and fire risks forward
segments.summary: Bringing fuel carriers toward danger raises spill, tank-layout, vapour, and damage-control questions that a replenishment plan must address.
segments.body: A tanker needed for wartime fuel distribution could cause a major spill if damaged. Planners might put ballast in vulnerable outer tanks when the ship operates closer to danger. Heavy ship fuel may not ignite readily on impact, but its release would still create a serious environmental hazard. Empty or partly emptied tanks can be more dangerous when fuel vapour mixes with oxygen and finds an ignition source. Cargo arrangement and damage control matter alongside transfer capacity.

evidence.note: The transcript raises the environmental consequences of tanker damage and the possibility of using ballast in outer tanks.
Fuel ignition, empty-tank vapour, oxygen, and operational planning are discussed as distinct hazards.

segments.title: MV Ocean Trader as a littoral support ship
segments.summary: MV Ocean Trader shows how a second-hand roll-on/roll-off hull can support helicopters, boats, drones, and special forces without pretending to be a high-threat warship.
segments.body: MV Ocean Trader offers a credible merchant conversion as a support ship. Its roll-on/roll-off hull provides hangar space, accommodation for up to 200 special-operations personnel, helicopter facilities, boats, and possible drone support. A medium power could use such a ship to extend the reach of an amphibious or littoral force. It cannot launch heavy landing craft and should not operate alone in a high-threat environment. Its value lies in carrying useful capabilities and spreading presence within those limits.

evidence.note: The transcript describes MV Ocean Trader, its Military Sealift Command conversion, and the appeal of a support ship for medium powers.
High-threat limitations, defensive options, helicopters, boats, and possible drone launch arrangements define the ship's practical role.

segments.title: Second-hand conversions begin with buyer beware
segments.summary: A cheap commercial hull is useful only after inspectors establish its service history, condition, and remaining structural life.
segments.body: Ocean Trader was available as a second-hand commercial vessel instead of being built to military order. That advantage depends on the hull retaining enough useful life to justify conversion and service costs. Buying it resembles purchasing a used aircraft or car because logs and seller disclosures cannot reveal every aspect of past use. The buyer needs a detailed inspection of the structure, machinery, and records before committing to military modifications. The seller's financial incentive makes that caution part of procurement.

evidence.note: The transcript links second-hand acquisition to remaining hull life and the need for a fine-tooth-comb inspection.
Seller disclosure, incomplete use history, records, visual inspection, and financial incentives underpin the buyer-beware warning.

segments.title: AIS silence can reveal a special-operations ship
segments.summary: A merchant-looking support ship gains range and carrying capacity, yet its AIS pattern can still advertise when operations become sensitive.
segments.body: MV Ocean Trader can carry larger boats, possible stealth submersibles, and helicopters, giving special forces more options than submarine insertion alone. At a distance, its commercial appearance helps it blend into ordinary traffic. Its Automatic Identification System track is watched, however, and disappearing from public tracking can signal that an operation is underway. Warships and auxiliaries can turn AIS off or use generic identities, but observers can still notice the pattern. Concealment depends on behavior and information discipline as much as hull shape.

evidence.note: The transcript links Ocean Trader tracking and AIS disappearance with special-operations activity, boats, submersibles, and helicopters.
Merchant-like appearance, AIS identification, generic naval identities, and transponder shutdown are explained.

segments.title: Low-threat patrol waters no longer stay low threat
segments.summary: Fishery and offshore patrol vessels need seakeeping, visibility, aviation, and stronger self-defence as drones and missiles spread beyond major powers.
segments.body: An offshore patrol vessel needs endurance, rough-weather seakeeping, a small crew, good all-round observation, and preferably a helicopter landing area. A modern fit could add a 57 mm gun, short-range missiles such as CAMM or ESSM, and perhaps a Phalanx close-in weapon system. Drones and accessible missiles have spread ranged attack beyond the states that once monopolized it. Waters previously classed as low threat may now expose patrol ships to weapons they were not designed to face. Those threats raise the minimum level of protection expected from an OPV.

evidence.note: The transcript sets out patrol-vessel seakeeping, crewing, visibility, helicopter, gun, missile, and close-in-defence requirements.
The spread of drones and missiles to more actors is used to explain why formerly low-threat patrol areas have changed.

segments.title: Platform supply vessels expose an OPV procurement choice
segments.summary: Commercial supply vessels often fit patrol needs and become available during energy downturns, but new OPV orders may be serving shipyard policy too.
segments.body: Platform supply vessels already possess many qualities wanted in an offshore patrol ship and are produced in large numbers for the energy industry. Market downturns can put more of them on the second-hand market when operators cut exploration or support activity. Navies repeatedly consider these vessels, then often choose a new-build OPV. A new order can preserve a specialist naval yard when the fleet is not buying enough warships to keep it busy. That creates a policy choice: either the yard is strategically necessary and needs steady work, or the fleet is ordering too few warships to sustain the industrial base it says it requires.

evidence.note: The transcript connects platform supply vessel availability with their production volume and fluctuations in energy markets.
New OPV construction is discussed as a means of sustaining naval shipyards when warship orders are insufficient.

segments.title: Supply vessels combine station-keeping, salvage, and deck space
segments.summary: Dynamic positioning, towing strength, and open working decks make platform supply vessels useful for salvage and rapid modular fits.
segments.body: Platform supply vessels are designed to loiter near offshore installations, often with excellent dynamic-positioning systems and some towing ability. Those characteristics also suit naval salvage, where damaged or immobilized warships must be pulled clear of danger. Navies demand salvage tugs quickly once combat begins because mission-damaged ships still need recovery. The large open afterdeck gives a supply vessel room for containerised or modular weapons and support equipment. A rapid conversion depends on stockpiling those modules before the crisis.

evidence.note: The transcript links station-keeping and tug functions with wartime salvage and removal of damaged ships from danger.
Open deck space is identified as well suited to pre-stockpiled containerized or modular equipment.

segments.title: Survey ships prepare the underwater battlespace
segments.summary: Oceanographic survey vessels map the seabed, support submarine recovery, and collect the coastal data needed before amphibious operations.
segments.body: The NOAA ship Ronald H. Brown shows the military value of civilian oceanographic survey vessels. Submarine forces depend on accurate seabed mapping, and a damaged submarine may require specialized search and recovery support below the surface. Amphibious forces need hydrographic knowledge of approaches and landing areas before committing an assault force. Existing peacetime surveys can provide some of that foundation, although a crisis may demand fresh work in a specific operating area. The resulting data directly shapes undersea and littoral operations.

evidence.note: The transcript uses Ronald H. Brown to discuss ocean-floor mapping and recovery of damaged submarines.
Survey work before amphibious operations is contrasted with relying on data gathered through continuing peacetime studies.

segments.title: Government ownership does not guarantee naval access
segments.summary: Civil-agency survey ships are already public assets, yet competing missions, departmental politics, and restoration demands can obstruct wartime transfer.
segments.body: Most survey vessels are owned by governments or arm's-length public agencies rather than navies. Legal access may be straightforward, yet practical transfer can be difficult because another department still has missions, political influence, and an expectation that its ship will return in usable condition. Wartime modifications may need to remain reversible. Planning during procurement is easier than negotiating every change after a crisis begins. A Danish survey ship, for example, could be designed to accept StanFlex modules and gain temporary military capabilities.

evidence.note: The transcript covers government ownership, departmental rivalry, continuing civilian missions, and demands for reversible changes.
Procurement-time preparation and a Danish StanFlex-compatible survey ship are offered as a practical solution.

segments.title: Survey ships already carry the computing a conversion needs
segments.summary: Survey vessels offer computing spaces that ordinary merchant ships lack, but weapons still require command, control, power, and survivability provisions.
segments.body: Ordinary merchant ships generally lack warship-standard sensors, electronics, subdivision, and combat survivability. Survey ships are an exception because their scientific mission already makes them floating data centers. Replacing or expanding some computers could create space for military command-and-control functions, especially if spare capacity was designed in from the start. A containerised launcher still needs a control system and may require a separate power module when ship connections are incompatible. As warfare compresses decision times from days to seconds, information must already be collected and synthesized.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts merchant survivability and electronics with the large computing installations carried by survey vessels.
Command containers, power compatibility, expansion space, and the accelerating speed of information in warfare are tied together.

segments.title: From Soviet intelligence trawlers to proxy-flagged covert craft
segments.summary: Small trawlers can watch naval forces, land covert teams, and hide ownership behind proxy companies and foreign flags.
segments.body: NATO carrier groups were once routinely followed by Soviet trawlers whose intelligence role was obvious even when they looked like fishing vessels. One image shows a trawler alongside USS Texas while monitoring the American cruiser. Modern sensors allow less conspicuous craft to collect information or support covert insertion with a small boat. Small crews are easier to control than a container ship's complement, while proxy companies and foreign registration can obscure the state directing them. AIS may reveal a trawler in an unlikely location without settling its ownership or intent. Non-state actors can also use small, rugged, deniable craft for surveillance or covert action.

evidence.note: The transcript recalls Soviet trawlers following NATO carrier groups and USS Texas as acknowledged intelligence assets.
Modern covert fits, small-boat insertion, AIS clues, proxy ownership, foreign flags, and non-state use are described.

segments.title: Reefers bring power and cranes to drone operations
segments.summary: Refrigerated cargo ships already distribute electrical power around their holds and decks, making them strong hosts for drones, mines, and modular systems.
segments.body: Refrigerated cargo ships, or reefers, already distribute electrical power to designated cargo positions around the ship. A containerised weapon system either needs that infrastructure or must devote additional containers to generators. Reefer layouts may also include cranes that can recover an uncrewed surface or underwater vessel for charging and maintenance. The same deck and handling features could support minelaying or other modular naval tasks. These built-in services make a reefer a more credible auxiliary conversion than a generic container ship.

evidence.note: The transcript explains reefer power connections, designated refrigerated-container positions, and the alternative of separate generator modules.
Cranes, drone charging, USV and UUV recovery, maintenance, and minelaying make reefers attractive auxiliary candidates.

segments.title: The most useful conversion may be the hardest ship to requisition
segments.summary: Reefers could covertly lay mines and host naval systems, but food and temperature-controlled trade already keep them in exceptional commercial demand.
segments.body: Reefers carry more than food because many goods need a constant temperature during transit. Commercial operators already face a persistent shortage of these ships, and wartime supply movements would increase demand further. Their normal port-to-port pattern, self-sufficiency, and handling gear could allow covert minelaying with uncertain attribution. The same characteristics make them among the easiest merchant ships to connect to containerised weapons and support systems. A navy might find that its best conversion candidate is too important to remove from civilian logistics.

evidence.note: The transcript emphasizes intense commercial demand for reefers and explains that temperature-controlled cargo extends beyond food.
Covert minelaying, historic wartime scarcity, rising supply demand, and the value of existing power distribution are connected.

segments.title: The modern requirement favors auxiliaries and protected shipping
segments.summary: The episode's answer rejects a broad return of armed merchant cruisers while preserving a case for supply-ship OPVs, auxiliaries, and protected wartime shipping.
segments.body: A modern navy has no general requirement for armed merchant cruisers. A platform supply vessel converted into an offshore patrol vessel comes closest, serving patrol and support roles rather than commerce raiding. Merchant shipping would still be indispensable during a large or prolonged war. Its contribution would depend on protection, preparation, and keeping specialized hulls in operation under threat. The practical requirement is for auxiliaries and defensible logistics.

evidence.note: The transcript gives a direct no to a general modern armed-merchant-cruiser tasking and identifies supply-ship OPV conversion as the nearest case.

segments.title: A crewed warship can anchor an uncrewed task group
segments.summary: Future frigates and destroyers can coordinate armed uncrewed escorts, but people remain essential for local control and repairs at sea.
segments.body: Future destroyers and frigates could become crewed centers of small task groups supported by uncrewed surface vessels carrying extra sensors and missiles. The uncrewed craft would spread firepower and create layered air defence, while the crewed combatant coordinates surface, air, and anti-submarine warfare much as a cruiser once coordinated smaller escorts. Keeping control local reduces pressure on vulnerable satellite communications. Helicopters and adequately sized crews could send maintenance parties when an uncrewed vessel breaks down. Robotics may eventually perform those repairs, but fleet plans should not assume that capability will arrive on schedule.

evidence.note: The transcript describes destroyers and frigates coordinating armed uncrewed escorts for air, surface, and anti-submarine warfare.
Satellite pressure, maintenance parties, limited repair robotics, and the danger of planning around immature technology are explained.

segments.title: Rawalpindi's torpedo counterfactual
segments.summary: HMS Rawalpindi's last fight supports a narrow counterfactual: torpedo batteries might have punished Scharnhorst and Gneisenau despite the converted liner's likely loss.
segments.body: HMS Rawalpindi was an armed merchant cruiser lost in an unequal fight with Scharnhorst and Gneisenau. In the counterfactual offered here, her close approach might have allowed four quintuple launchers to fire ten torpedoes at each German ship. Such spreads would have been difficult to comb even if Rawalpindi were still sunk. A narrow tactical armament could therefore have let the converted liner damage or sink one of its much stronger opponents.

evidence.note: The transcript considers how four quintuple torpedo launchers on Rawalpindi might have changed her engagement with Scharnhorst and Gneisenau.

segments.title: Last-mile defence must exist before the emergency
segments.summary: Containerized defensive missiles and Phalanx-like systems offer more value than large offensive batteries, provided maritime fits and stockpiles are prepared in advance.
segments.body: Large offensive missile loads use merchant deck space poorly, whereas smaller defensive missiles could be containerised in useful numbers. Close-in weapon systems could provide another layer of last-mile protection against threats that pass through area defence. The land-based Phalanx systems used for base defence in Iraq and Afghanistan raise practical questions about salt-water operation, shipboard installation, and retention in reserve. A maritime fit would have to be prepared and qualified before a crisis. The ability to bolt a system onto a ship has little value if no stockpile is available.

evidence.note: The transcript favors compact defensive missiles and close-in weapons over space-inefficient offensive missile loads.
Land-based Phalanx use leads to questions about salt-water adaptation, retention, and rapid fitting to merchant vessels.

segments.title: Hormuz turns merchant self-defence into a current problem
segments.summary: The Strait of Hormuz case separates the mine threat from drones and missiles that rapidly fitted close-in defences could help merchant ships survive.
segments.body: The March 2026 Strait of Hormuz situation makes the preparation problem immediate. Mines are the primary Iranian threat discussed here, and Phalanx or short-range missiles cannot solve that hazard. Those systems could give merchant crews more confidence against missiles and drones. Large attack drones should be visible to airborne warning and regional defences, while smaller threats that slip through may fall inside a ship's close-in engagement envelope. Merchant self-defence depends on having systems ready for rapid fitting.

evidence.note: The transcript applies merchant-ship Phalanx and missile fits to mines, missiles, and drones in the Strait of Hormuz.
Modern forces are contrasted with the reserve guns that could arm merchant ships during the world wars.

segments.title: A defensive fit inherits the ship's flag problem
segments.summary: Multinational ownership and flags of convenience complicate hardpoint standards, armed guards, command relationships, and rules of engagement.
segments.body: Preparing merchant ships for missile defence requires builders to provide hard points, power, and interfaces before weapons are needed. Earlier British and American systems could incentivize nationally flagged fleets, then draw weapons from government stockpiles during war. Modern ships may be owned, chartered, registered, and flagged in different countries, making a common requirement difficult to impose. Armed guards and weapon systems would be easier to govern on a national or allied flag because command relationships and rules of engagement remain clearer. Economic flagging decisions therefore become security constraints during mobilization.

evidence.note: The transcript asks what builders should prepare and contrasts historic national hardpoint programs with multinational ownership and registration.
Allied flags, armed guards, command, rules of engagement, flag-state territory, and economically driven registration are discussed.

segments.title: Merchant hulls can deploy off-board mine systems
segments.summary: Traditional minesweeping trawlers give way to uncrewed off-board systems, but navies still need suitable ships to carry, launch, and recover them.
segments.body: Trawlers were traditionally requisitioned for wartime minesweeping, while modern mine countermeasures increasingly move sensors and clearance tools off board. The Royal Navy has capable uncrewed systems but too few ships from which to deploy them. A merchant conversion could carry those systems into the operating area. Reefers are attractive because their cranes and distributed power suit uncrewed craft and modular equipment. Intense commercial demand may keep those ships beyond naval reach when a crisis also strains civilian supply.

evidence.note: The transcript moves from historic trawler minesweeping to British off-board systems, deployment-ship shortages, and the appeal but scarcity of reefers.

segments.title: Just-in-time shipping leaves no mobilization cushion
segments.summary: Modern trade has too little spare shipping to requisition auxiliaries without economic shock, as the Falklands campaign already demonstrated.
segments.body: The lack of spare capacity in the merchant fleet is the largest constraint on wartime conversion. World War I and World War II mobilization could draw on more slack, while Britain's 1982 Falklands requisitions already created major commercial ripples. Just-in-time logistics, procurement, and shipping minimize cost while every link functions normally. The same efficiency removes the reserve capacity needed to absorb war or other disruptions, as COVID-19 and Suez Canal crises demonstrated. A navy cannot plan merchant auxiliaries by counting hulls alone because taking those ships from trade may undermine the economy and military supply chain they are meant to support.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts current merchant-fleet capacity with the world wars and the economic effects of Falklands requisitions.
Just-in-time efficiency is identified as particularly vulnerable to disruption because it retains no slack.
